observation: Rayner et al. 2016 (comprehensive review across eye-tracking, RSVP, and applied speed-reading-program studies) found radically faster reading (500-1000+ wpm) does not preserve comprehension; the speed/comprehension tradeoff is a hard constraint from visual/cognitive architecture (foveal acuity, saccade/fixation limits), not a trainable skill gap.
claim: Speed reading (read much faster with equal comprehension) is debunked; Riemann should never advertise a fast-pass mode as 'read faster, understand the same.'
mechanism: Foveal visual acuity and saccade/fixation timing are physiological constraints on how fast text can be accurately parsed, independent of training.
context: comprehensive review across eye-tracking, RSVP, and applied program studies

implications.text: If Riemann offers a fast pass through a document (skim mode, RSVP-style flashing), be explicit in the UI that it trades comprehension depth for speed, rather than promising equal comprehension at higher speed.

observation: The same Rayner et al. 2016 review explicitly separates 'get through it fast with moderate comprehension' (skimming) from 'speed-read with full comprehension' (debunked), framing skimming as a legitimate strategy when thorough understanding isn't the goal.
claim: Skimming for a lower, explicit comprehension target is a legitimate, non-cheating strategy Riemann can design for directly -- this validates the whole premise of offering L0/L1 as genuine, adequate stopping points rather than merely compressed previews of a 'real' L3 read.
context: same comprehensive review, authors' own framing

implications.text: Present L0/L1 as legitimate, complete-in-themselves comprehension targets ('skim for gist') rather than as an inferior stand-in for reading the whole document.

observation: Brysbaert 2019 meta-analysis (190 studies, 18,573 participants, fact-checked confirmed) found average adult silent reading rate ~238 wpm for non-fiction, ~260 wpm fiction, ~183 wpm oral reading; word length is a significant moderator (longer words in non-fiction lower the rate).
claim: Riemann's time-estimate UI should use ~230-260 wpm (not 300+), and ideally expose a difficulty-adjusted multiplier since jargon density/sentence length shifts the effective rate down further.
context: large meta-analysis spanning over a century of reading-rate data

implications.text: Use 238 wpm (non-fiction) as the base rate for any 'this will take you N minutes' UI, with a difficulty-adjusted multiplier for jargon-dense content.

observation: Bloom's revised taxonomy is a two-dimensional grid (knowledge type x cognitive process/verb complexity) classifying what task a learner can perform, not a model of representation depth; it is a stable, widely-used educational classification scheme, not an empirically validated causal/psychological model.
claim: Bloom's taxonomy measures a different thing than Riemann's L0-L3 abstraction depth (which is a Kintsch-style representation-depth ladder, not a task-capability ladder); if Sam wants Bloom-style capability targets ('I need to be able to apply this'), the ladder needs a second, orthogonal axis.
context: stable, widely-used classification scheme, not itself an experimentally validated model

implications.text: Do not conflate abstraction-depth (L0-L3) with task-capability targets in Riemann's design language; if a Bloom-style capability target is ever added, model it as a separate axis from zoom depth.

observation: SOLO taxonomy (Biggs & Collis: prestructural, unistructural, multistructural, relational, extended abstract) measures the structural quality of a response (how many relevant aspects are used and whether integrated), independent of Bloom's verb list, and was designed as a more observable/practical alternative.
claim: SOLO's depth levels (unistructural through extended abstract) offer a plausible mapping for Riemann's 'target depth' concept, loosely aligned to L0-L3 but conceptually distinct from pure representation depth.
context: widely used in education, less quantitatively validated than cognitive-science models

implications.text: Model 'target depth' as a small set of named goals (gist / working understanding / can-teach-it) loosely aligned to SOLO levels, each with an estimated time budget, rather than a single unlabeled zoom position.

observation: Kintsch's construction-integration model posits three levels of mental representation during reading: surface form (exact wording, decays fast), textbase (propositions/ideas as structured by the text), and situation model (integration of textbase with the reader's prior knowledge, associated with true durable comprehension and transfer).
claim: Riemann's L0-L3 tree should be designed against Kintsch's model: L0/L1 should preserve situation-model content (meaning, relations, why it matters) over textbase content (exact propositions); L2 is closer to textbase (structured but not yet integrated); L3 is the only level with surface/verbatim fidelity.
mechanism: Durable comprehension and transfer depend on situation-model integration, not on retaining exact wording (surface form), which decays fastest.
population: general readers (foundational, decades of replicated cognitive-science follow-up)

implications.text: Optimize L0/L1 generation prompts for gist/situation-model quality (a reader who only sees L0 should be able to reason about the content, not just recite a topic label) and have L2 preserve document structure/signposting rather than compress it away.

observation: Fuzzy-trace theory (Reyna & Brainerd) holds gist (semantic/meaning) and verbatim (surface-form) memory traces are encoded, stored, and forgotten in parallel and largely independently; gist traces are more durable and are what people actually use for reasoning and decisions, while verbatim traces decay quickly.
claim: L0/L1 (gist-level) content is a strong theoretical candidate for the level users should return to for durable retention, not just for initial speed -- gist is not merely a lossy compression of verbatim, it is the more durable and more used representation.
mechanism: Gist and verbatim traces are stored via separate memory processes with different decay rates, so a well-formed gist is not simply an impoverished verbatim trace but a distinct, more durable representation.

implications.text: Treat L0/L1 as legitimate targets for spaced-return/retrieval-practice features (not just L3), since gist traces -- not verbatim -- are the durable representation people actually use.

observation: Advance-organizer meta-analyses (1980s, with known heterogeneity/inconsistent operationalization) find effect sizes vary hugely by organizer type: graphic organizers show ~1.24 effect, while plain expository-text organizers show only ~0.2-0.3.
claim: L2 (section gists) should function as a structural/graphic pre-organiser (visible hierarchy, headers, indentation, spatial layout) before a user commits to L3, since graphic organizers meta-analytically far outperform prose organizers.
mechanism: A graphic organiser makes hierarchical/relational structure directly visible before detailed reading, letting the reader build an anticipatory schema to slot subsequent detail into.
population: general learners (1980s meta-analyses, heterogeneous study inclusion)
context: old meta-analyses with known heterogeneity issues; treat the 1.24 figure as suggestive, not a performance target

implications.text: Render L2 with visible hierarchy/structure (headers, indentation, spatial layout) rather than as prose paragraphs, functioning as a graphic pre-organiser for L3.

observation: Pan & Carpenter's 2023 review found pretesting/prequestions (answering questions before reading, then seeing correct answers) improves subsequent learning even when learners get most items wrong at first, provided feedback follows; the effect is attentional (prequestions direct visual attention/fixations, shown via eye-tracking) and robust across adulthood, but works better for factual than conceptual material.
claim: A single, cheap, auto-generated prequestion at an L0-to-L1 or L1-to-L2 transition is a low-cost, evidence-backed germane-load technique, but it should target specific checkable facts/claims rather than broad 'what is this about' conceptual questions to stay in the effect's better-supported range.
mechanism: Answering a question before reading directs subsequent visual attention/fixations toward the content needed to answer it, even when the initial guess is wrong.
population: general adult readers (multiple converging studies; robustness-across-adulthood specifically confirmed)
context: multiple converging studies and a 2023 review; smaller literature than Dunlosky's headline techniques

implications.text: Surface a single auto-generated prequestion targeting a specific fact/claim before expanding a section, at low friction, rather than a broad conceptual question.

observation: Dunlosky et al. 2013 rate practice testing and distributed practice as high-utility techniques (broad age ranges, material types, robust effects); elaborative interrogation, self-explanation, and interleaved practice as moderate utility; summarization, highlighting/underlining, keyword mnemonic, imagery, and rereading as low utility for general use. A 2021 meta-analysis broadly confirms the ranking.
claim: Retrieval practice and spaced/distributed practice are the highest-leverage optional add-ons for durable understanding, but they add real time cost and should sit behind an explicit 'remember this later' toggle, separate from the default 'understand this now' zoom-dial flow.
population: general learners across ages and material types (synthesis of decades of research)
context: landmark synthesis published in Psychological Science in the Public Interest, plus a confirming 2021 meta-analysis

implications.text: Put retrieval-practice/spaced-return features behind an explicit opt-in 'remember this later' toggle, distinct from the default fast-comprehension zoom-dial path, since Dunlosky's utility ratings are for durable retention, not fast one-off understanding.

observation: The expertise reversal effect (Kalyuga 2007, a robust and repeatedly-replicated CLT effect, with a 2025 meta-analysis quantifying it directly) shows instructional supports that help novices (worked examples, heavy scaffolding) become neutral or actively harmful for learners with higher prior domain knowledge, because the scaffolding itself becomes extraneous load once schemas already exist.
claim: Riemann should adapt scaffolding depth, not just requested zoom depth, to detected prior knowledge: if the system can infer the user already knows the domain, it should skip L1/L2 hand-holding and let them land closer to L3 directly, since extra structure for an expert is friction, not help.
mechanism: Scaffolding/extra structure occupies working-memory capacity that a novice needs to build a schema but that an expert, who already has the schema, experiences as pure extraneous (redundant) load.
population: learners across expertise levels (robust, repeatedly-replicated CLT effect)

implications.text: Infer prior-knowledge level (past interaction history, or a quick calibration question) and use it to set default dial position/scaffolding depth, not just to respond to an explicitly requested depth.

observation: No single technique/level in this report's literature is 'correct' in isolation; achieving a target depth within a time budget is structurally a search over a path through L0-L3 plus optional cheap technique add-ons (prequestion: seconds; retrieval check: ~1 min; self-summary: ~1-2 min) with known, differing incremental payoffs.
claim: Riemann should model 'target depth + time budget' as a small search/allocation problem (pick a path through levels plus optional add-ons), not a single fixed pipeline, letting the dial choose the shortest path that hits the target depth.
population: n/a (synthesis/design-framing observation, not a single empirical claim)
context: synthesis across the report's own findings, not itself a cited study

implications.text: Design the abstraction-tree navigation as a budget-allocation model: named depth targets (gist / working understanding / can-teach-it) each with an estimated base time plus optional technique add-ons with known incremental payoff.

observation: Dunlosky et al.'s utility ratings are calibrated for durable, long-term learning (the classroom/exam use case), whereas Riemann's primary objective per the brief is often 'understand now, in the shortest time' -- a different objective function where high-retention-utility techniques like spaced practice are actively the wrong choice.
claim: Dunlosky's technique-utility ratings should not be imported wholesale as 'what Riemann should always do'; they answer 'what should I do to remember this in a month,' not 'what's the fastest path to today's understanding,' and the two goals should be kept visibly separate in the product.
population: general learners (same Dunlosky synthesis, reinterpreted for a different objective)
context: same synthesis as F05-10, reframed as a caveat about objective mismatch

implications.text: Keep 'fast comprehension now' and 'durable retention later' as two visibly distinct modes/toggles in Riemann, rather than applying retention-oriented techniques by default to the fast-understanding path.
